I'm starting to come around more to this notion of the film being a satirical meta-reflection on Fincher himself. The ultimate message though would be something similar to the ending of "The Hurt Locker" (which also seemed to be self-referential on Bigelow), where it's all about the work, and how that's the one thing they truly enjoy doing at the expense of everything else in their life. Like others have stated, even if this is what the movie truly is, it still wasn't as intriguing/stimulating/enjoyable as Fincher's other works, nor did it have a fluid, satisfying integration between allegory and story. The best satires seem to walk that razor's edge between being obvious enough where you don't need to put a lot of effort in pointing out what it's really about, and in not coming off as preachy at the same time (like say, "Don't Look Up").
If we take this movie as a comment on Fincher himself, it does seem like one of the core messages is Fincher pointing out that he's slipping, and perhaps even thinking about hanging it up.

It's absolutely a formalist exercise in cinematic storytelling technique above all else. Like Rope or Rear Window, it pushes what was achievable with the technology at the time within certain deliberate parameters to make audiences feel a certain way. The Panic Room is arguably the theatre itself as he cranks up the tension purely through tricks and technique. There's no other aspect to the film except this formalist structure in service to tension. The lead characters' surname is also Altman. A director known for a much looser approach, yet no less technologically innovative...

The Game is even more explicit in its deconstruction of thriller tropes and cinematic tricks to dispense information, ideas and experiences to audiences. It doesn't play fair from the get go. It's all ultimately an expensive thrill ride ruse designed to hopefully teach Michael Douglas something profound about his life. Whether or not it actually does is left open...

For what it's worth I don't think Panic Room, The Game or The Killer are entirely successful. Although enjoyable, they collapse under the weight of their intent for me and don't completely stack up. But I can see what he's trying to do and think the ideas are solid.

 I can see it easily becoming the association people will casually make about it for years, but really I take Fincher at his word that he just wanted to make a straight up vintage B-movie about an assassin:

>The Killer is really just a modern version of a vintage B movie. Mention this to Fincher and Walker, and both will agree that that’s exactly what they were going for. The director recalls going to Netflix before they began production and telling them, “I’m going to do it stripped-down. This is a Don Siegel movie. It’s a fucking Michael Winner movie. It’s Charley Varrick, Get Carter, The Mechanic. This is meant to be ballistic.” Even the rapid-fire credits sequence that opens the film was meant to evoke the tough-guy procedurals of yesteryear. “The style can be described as: a Quinn-Martin production,” he says, bursting into laughter. “It’s Mannix chic.”

https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-features/david-fincher-the-killer-interview-michael-fassbender-netflix-1234865655/

I found the film enjoyable but hollow the first watch, and after reading more of Fincher's actual intent behind it, I've appreciated it more on rewatch:

>“But here’s the thing,” he says. “The question we asked ourselves going in was: Could you hitch a ride with a sociopath who may not have a lot of emotional bandwidth, make it an intensely subjective experience, but still give somebody something that’s compelling to watch, rather than repulsing them? And I think it’s an effective invocation of what we were trying to do by that criteria. I’ve done movies that have twists and turns, and maybe people are waiting for that stuff. Andy and I didn’t want to make a maze. We wanted to make an arrow: something that flies straight in one direction and hits a target.

That's a great catch. Nobody notices pop cultural references from series that were huge in syndication because none of them are available to stream these days. The streaming libraries now dictate the pop cultural canon and drive the  discourse. Monoculture is all pervasive and too much deviation is regarded with suspicion and derision. Suddenly strange glitches appear, like the recent online appreciation of After Hours as iconoclastic opinion, and the flock moves as one in murmuration. Puzzling.

The internet has been responsible for an epidemic of education worn lightly and highly contagious infected information. The haemorrhage of Media Studies buzz words and concepts that bleed out online actually mask a downturn in media literacy. 

There is no anti-memetics division. The falconer cannot see the falcon. Soundbites are loosed, shorn of all context. Wild theories proliferate and form into facts creating feedback loops of fractured data. Room 237 leads to pizza parlour basements containing adrenochrome extraction facilities.  

A little learning is a dangerous thing, as the actual Pope quote goes...

I'm the person who brought up the point about the branding being purposeful, and I saw the film in an indie university theatre. It was that experience which helped me form my opinion that Fincher has grown/developed brilliantly as an aesthetic auteur but very poorly as a storyteller/someone who can merge visuals and script to promote a theme.

No one in my theatre was laughing at the Killer. They were laughing with him. Which is, fundamentally from everything the script and plot tells us, wrong. The framing and technical substance exudes a particular cool aloofness which is classic Fincher; the problem of watching it in person with others was seeing in real time how easy it is to misconstrue what seems to be the point with that idea's diametric opposite. AKA, the exact same thing that happened with Fight Club.

I love Fincher's work and was really excited for The Killer. But I do think it fails fundamentally on that level.

My wife and I saw it in theaters, as well. However it was a relatively empty theater. I wasn't really sitting in proximity to the few people there so I could not decipher their reactions but my wife and I did laugh and rib each other during the moments we found funny throughout. I'm not sure what the observation says about noticing what other people are laughing at other than the notion that humor is subjective. I'm not going to judge an audience member (or filmmaker) because they laughed at a moment I didn't think was funny or shouldn't be worth their laugh.

My point isn’t that they were laughing at something I didn’t find funny; the subjective interpretation of a moment in a film, whether it’s comedic or dramatic or some intersection of those things, matters. Fight Club being so misconstrued that people literally went out to form fight clubs was very much on people misinterpreting the films message, but also reflected something of a failure in Finchers style and vision.

I’m mostly responding to the idea that people with under-formed or bad takes didn’t see it in the ‘proper’ setting, like a theatre, where their attention was monopolised by what was on screen. Divergent takes can also happen in those spaces, and sometimes that’s down to the filmmaker.
